comment: What must not silently disappear from gmailtriage. `prose` names guardrails no code enforces; `split` declares which half of the skill is deterministic; `baseline` names the offline, $0 checks pinned against a real run.

prose.pattern: A message is trashed only because a rule the user wrote matc
prose.rationale: The one rule. It is the reason this skill exists rather than a prompt; lose the line and the skill becomes a generic assistant with extra steps.

prose.pattern: Never claim a result you did not observe
prose.rationale: Honesty about what was verified is the whole house contract. A skill that reports success it did not witness is worse than one that reports nothing.

prose.pattern: Never trash a thread the plan did not name
prose.rationale: The scaffolded invariant here was about a detect step this skill does not have. This is the one that matters: the plan is the authorisation, and a thread outside it has no rule behind it. Lose this line and `apply` becomes advisory.

prose.pattern: Never move a thread the plan did not name, and never under an action it did
prose.rationale: The sort half of the one rule. A plan that authorises filing a thread into a folder must not equally authorise trashing it — same thread id, same plan, catastrophically different outcome. Lose this line and the two actions collapse into one permission, which is how sorting becomes a way around every trash guard in the skill.

prose.pattern: Never invent a folder name silently
prose.rationale: Naming an unhoused cluster is the one judgment call sorting adds, and it belongs to the user. A skill that guesses files a school district into a folder named after its mail vendor, and mail the user cannot find is mail the user has lost.

Trash is recoverable for 30 days and the MCP has no permanent delete. Calling it deletion overstates the risk to the user and, worse, invites someone to 'fix' the skill by reaching for a destructive operation that does not exist. Since 0.2.0 the same line covers archiving, which is not destructive at all.

prose.pattern: Never leave a folder unmanaged without saying so
prose.rationale: A folder no rule files into stays sorted exactly as long as the user keeps sorting it by hand, and nothing in Gmail ever mentions it. Lose this line and the skill maintains half a mailbox while reporting success over the whole thing — which is worse than maintaining none, because the user stops checking.

prose.pattern: Never delete a label with mail in it, and never delete one on your own
prose.rationale: Deleting an empty folder loses nothing; deleting one holding mail loses the only record of why that mail was kept together, and no receipt can reconstruct it. `merge` exists precisely so a folder with mail in it never has to be deleted.

prose.pattern: Never name a sub-label after the sender when the sender hosts mail
prose.rationale: Splitting a folder into sub-labels re-opens the exact failure the folder-naming rule closed: an applicant tracking system, a signing service or an invoicing platform sends for whoever bought it, so the address names the vendor and the subject names the organisation. Lose this line and `Recruiting/Ashbyhq` files every employer into one folder — the school-district-under-its-mail-vendor bug, committed by the fix for it.

prose.pattern: Never let a broad rule stand in front of a rule filing into a sub-label
prose.rationale: This pair does not fail, it drifts — fresh mail takes the parent rule and mail already filed skips it and takes the child, so which folder a thread lands in depends only on when it arrived and nothing reports it. Lose this line and nesting silently produces two half-filled folders out of one rule set.

prose.pattern: the guard is on what the skill suggests
prose.rationale: The withheld list is about what the skill proposes, never about what the user may decide. Losing the distinction turns a helpful default into a tool that argues with its owner.

prose.pattern: Never re-print a snippet or a code from a tool result
prose.rationale: The one leak the deterministic half cannot close. search_threads returns message snippets alongside subjects, and on a real mailbox those snippets have carried live verification codes — twice. The tool result entering the transcript is outside this skill's control; the model repeating it is not. ingest structurally never writes a snippet to disk; this line is the same guarantee for the conversation.

prose.pattern: never transcribe a tool response by hand
prose.rationale: Hand-transcribing search_threads output into threads.json was 60-90 seconds per run and the main way a field got dropped or mangled — measured across five real runs. The agent's only job at the fetch boundary is to write the tool result to a scratchpad file byte-for-byte; `ingest` owns the reshaping, deterministically. Lose this line and the hand-built JSON quietly comes back, and with it the transcription errors ingest exists to end.

prose.pattern: Never propose a rule for a sender an existing rule already claims
prose.rationale: `propose` clustered on senders with no knowledge of the rule set, so it re-proposed rules for mail the user had already ruled on. The noise was the mild half: on a live mailbox it proposed TRASHING a sender whose mail an existing SORT rule was filing, which would have binned real-estate signing documents the user had deliberately kept. Same defect class as `audit-does-not-call-filed-mail-unclaimed`, and the same remedy — `matches(..., { ignoreFiled: true })`, because a thread already sitting in the folder its rule files into is the MOST claimed thread in the mailbox, not an unclaimed one. Claimed at SENDER granularity: a rule claiming only some of a sender's mail still proves the user has decided about that sender, and the leftovers are exactly what would otherwise cluster into a trash rule sitting in front of their sort rule.

deterministic.step: report whether this mailbox has any rules yet, and the single next thing to do — the only command safe to run before anything is configured

normalize raw search_threads and list_labels tool output, written to files verbatim, into the thread and label snapshots every other command reads — deduping threads across fetches, unioning label ids, deriving category and the bulk-mail proxy from the category id-sets, counting self-sent mail, refusing a metadata-only fetch by name, and never writing a snippet to disk

report whether the label system is still coherent — folders no rule manages, split into ones holding mail and empty scaffolding; rules that file into a folder that no longer exists; pairs of labels that are one folder spelled two ways, including transpositions; and mail no rule claims, self-sent mail excluded and counted — returning a coverage percentage and exiting non-zero while anything is outstanding

fold one folder into another in the only safe order — apply the target label, then remove the source, then delete the source folder — and write a receipt even when no mail moved, so the deleted folder can be restored
cluster a real inbox sample into trash candidates and sort candidates, matching each sort cluster against the labels the mailbox already has

cluster a folder that already has mail in it by sender domain, match each cluster against the sub-labels that folder already has, flag the senders that host mail for many organisations, and say when the folder is still one thing

validate, store and remove rules — compiling each to a Gmail query, refusing one that is malformed, matches everything, matches nothing, files into a label Gmail owns, or stands in front of a rule filing into a sub-label of its own destination, backing the previous file up before every write, and refusing to remove a rule id that does not exist
reconcile every folder the rules file into against the mailbox's real labels, and refuse to pass until each one exists

evaluate the stored rules against a named slice of the mailbox — the inbox by default, or a folder already filed — and enumerate exactly which threads each rule would take, every label each one applies, which of those the thread does not already carry, and which leave the inbox, without touching any of them
authorise exactly the threads the plan named, per action, refuse anything it did not, and write a receipt of every move
reverse every move listed in a previous run's receipt — untrash, unlabel, and put back in the inbox

nondeterministic.step: decide which proposed rules are actually safe to accept, and which cluster is a newsletter the user genuinely reads
nondeterministic.why: a sender sending fifty near-identical bulk messages looks the same whether it is a retailer the user ignores or the school district they need; only the user knows which

nondeterministic.step: name a folder for a cluster that has no existing home
nondeterministic.why: a folder name is a decision about how the user already thinks — whether their word is "Shopping" or "Retail", whether the bank goes under "Finance" or its own name — and nothing in the mail says it; a script that guesses files a school district under its mail vendor

nondeterministic.step: decide whether an unmanaged folder should be adopted with a rule or deleted
nondeterministic.why: a folder holding real mail with no rule behind it wants a rule and an empty one is scaffolding, the remedies are opposite, and the thread count only says which is likely — a folder emptied last week still means something

nondeterministic.step: decide which of two spellings of one folder is the right one
nondeterministic.why: the skill can prove two labels are one folder; nothing on disk says whether the user's word is "Receipts" or "Reciepts", and folding mail into the misspelling puts it somewhere they will never think to look

nondeterministic.step: name the organisation behind a sender that hosts mail for many of them
nondeterministic.why: an applicant tracking system, a signing service and an invoicing platform all send on behalf of whoever bought them, so the address names the vendor and the subject names the organisation; no-reply@ashbyhq.com is Obvious in one thread and someone else in the next, and only reading the subject says which

nondeterministic.step: decide whether a folder is several things or still one
nondeterministic.why: four employers in Recruiting want splitting and four notices from one bank in Statements do not, and the counts look identical either way; a sub-label holding everything its parent holds has given one pile two names rather than organising anything

nondeterministic.step: word each rule so a reader six months later can tell what it was meant to catch
nondeterministic.why: a Gmail query is precise and unreadable, and a rule nobody can interpret is a rule nobody will dare to edit

nondeterministic.step: judge when a plan looks wrong and should be questioned rather than applied
nondeterministic.why: a rule that suddenly matches ten times its usual volume is either a sender gone rogue or a rule that drifted, and nothing in the count itself says which

_baseline_comment: Offline and $0 by construction: no network, no model, so CI cannot spend and cannot flake. The corpus is INVENTED, not a redacted mailbox — this skill's fixtures would otherwise be somebody's private mail, and pseudonymising the senders still leaves the shape of a person's life in a public repo. Every domain sits under a reserved TLD and scripts/tests/no-real-data.test.mjs fails the build if that stops being true. What the goldens pin is the SHAPE of a real run — cluster sizes, which senders trip which guard, a folder that wants splitting, a folder spelled two ways, mail no rule claims — reproduced by evals/baseline/make-corpus.mjs.

baseline.rationale: the rule compiler or the planner silently changing which threads a rule takes, while still emitting a complete-looking plan — pinned against a frozen synthetic corpus shaped after a real triage run — propose, rules and plan re-run and byte-compared.
the one rule failing silently — the model, or a bug, trashing something no rule named — pinned against a receipt-producing apply run handed a thread id absent from its plan.
a malformed or over-broad rule reaching apply, which is how one bad rule empties an inbox — pinned against a rule whose compiled query is empty or matches the entire mailbox.

sorting becoming a way around every trash guard in the skill — a rule declaring {"action":"label","label":"TRASH"} destroys mail through the one action that exists so nothing is destroyed, and no trash guard is looking at a label rule. Pinned against a rule set naming TRASH, SPAM and CATEGORY_PROMOTIONS as destinations.

the two actions collapsing into one permission — a plan that authorises filing a thread into a folder must not authorise trashing it, since it is the same thread id in the same plan with a catastrophically different outcome. Pinned against a real plan whose label-rule thread ids are handed to apply as a trash list.

the sub-label half silently ceasing to work — pinned against a synthetic retroactive run shaped after a real one over a Recruiting folder: subdivide clustering it, and plan re-evaluating the rules against `label:Recruiting` rather than the inbox, both re-run and byte-compared. Catches a cluster losing its home, a vendor-hosted sender being auto-named after its vendor, the parent label dropping out of a sub-label's path, and the retroactive plan reporting archives it would never perform.

a retroactive pass that never finishes — re-planning the frozen Recruiting folder with its sub-labels already applied must take ZERO threads. If label ids stop resolving to names, or the already-filed short-circuit stops firing, every run re-proposes everything the last one filed and the skill silently never converges while every table still looks correct.

the drift that nesting invites — a rule filing into a folder standing ahead of one filing into a sub-label of it does not fail, it splits the mailbox by arrival time. Pinned two-sided against a rule set carrying that exact pair, which must be refused, and the corrected set, which must pass — so the check cannot be satisfied by refusing nesting outright.

the audit silently ceasing to find what it exists to find — pinned against a synthetic label list and rule set shaped after a real mailbox BEFORE the hygiene pass (5 unmanaged folders, one transposed duplicate pair, 16 unclaimed threads) and AFTER it (100% coverage, clean, exit 0), both re-run and byte-compared. Catches the unmanaged/duplicate/unclaimed classification drifting, the coverage arithmetic changing, and the clean state ceasing to be reachable.

the defect the second live run had: `propose` never read the rule file, so it re-proposed rules for mail already covered — including a TRASH candidate for a sender an existing SORT rule was filing. Pinned two-sided by two frozen runs over the SAME corpus: `propose.txt` uses rules-none.json (a genuine first run, everything proposed) and `propose-covered.txt` uses rules.json (every sender claimed, nothing proposed, the exclusion reported by name). The pair is what proves the filter fires on coverage and not on the corpus. `rules-none.json` is explicit rather than absent on purpose — `propose` defaults to ~/.gmailtriage/rules.json, so an implicit first run would read whoever ran refresh.sh.

the defect the first live audit had: it reused `plan`, which answers "is there work to do" and says no for a thread already sitting in the folder its rule files into — the most claimed thread in the mailbox. That reported 47 of 48 threads as unclaimed, rendering a clean mailbox as a broken one. Pinned two-sided: the frozen audit must find the real orphans and must NOT find the correctly-filed mail.

a hygiene check that is decorative in either direction. Pinned two-sided against the real transposed pair, which must be caught, and against short and genuinely-different label names, which must not be — a check that reports false pairs stops being read, and then the real pair goes unnoticed too.

a fixture refresh collapsing the corpus to a handful of threads, so the golden passes over almost nothing — pinned against the frozen thread corpus, label list and rule set, with a declared minimum count.

the normalizer silently drifting — a dedupe that stops unioning label ids, a category intersection that stops firing, a first-message rule that changes which sender a thread reports — while the output still looks like a thread list. Pinned by the frozen ingest run over raw MCP-shaped fixtures, byte-compared like every other golden.

the one field that has carried live verification codes being persisted. The raw fixtures plant a fake code in every message snippet, and the frozen ingest output is grepped for both the field and the content — so a refactor that starts copying messages wholesale fails the moment it lands, not the first time a real code is written to somebody's disk.

the 08-09 failure re-armed: a THREAD_VIEW_METADATA_ONLY fetch has no senders or subjects, and ingesting it produces ghost threads a later audit reports as unclaimed mail. The refusal must name the cause and write nothing; --force is the documented override and must keep working, or the refusal becomes a wall instead of a gate.

the owner's own outbox reported as mail no rule claims, which kept audit exiting non-zero forever on clean mailboxes — a gate that can never be satisfied stops being read. Two-sided: a mailbox whose only unclaimed mail is self-sent must audit CLEAN, and a genuine stranger beside it must still count. The corpus carries two SENT-only threads so the frozen audit-after golden proves the clean state stays reachable.

a real run wrote its thread snapshot into this skill's own checkout, and the cleanup deleted the run's receipt with it — that run is permanently un-undoable. Every data output now refuses a path inside a git working tree, with --allow-repo as the explicit override; the trap proves the refusal fires, the override works, and a plain temp dir never trips it.

the mid-run hand-edits coming back. apply --update-threads replays the authorised moves onto the working snapshot; a re-plan over it must take zero threads, or every mid-run rule addition costs hand-edited JSON again — and a hand-edit that seeds resolved label names wrong is exactly how a run stops converging while every table still reads correctly.

the reverse of the unmanaged-folder question, found live: a user deletes a folder, the rule pointing at it survives, and audit reported the system clean over it — coherence claimed in one direction only. Two-sided against the frozen corpus: the before-state carries a rule filing into a folder its label list does not have and must be called out; the after-state drops it and must still audit clean with exit 0, so the check cannot be satisfied by reporting findings unconditionally.

rule removal arriving without its guarantees. Before 0.7.0 the only way to drop a rule was hand-editing the validated store — the exact thing the store exists to prevent. The trap pins: exactly the named rules go, a byte-complete backup lands beside the file first, the remainder still validates, an unknown id is refused rather than silently skipped, and --add with --remove is refused as two intents in one invocation.

real mail getting back into a public repo. Every corpus file is checked for a sender domain outside the reserved TLDs and for any organisation this mailbox actually deals with, and the generated fixtures are re-run and byte-compared so a hand-edited one fails — hand-editing is how a real address gets pasted in. Lives in its own file because `skillfactory freeze` rewrites baseline.test.mjs, and this is the guard that must survive a refresh.
